upload.title: Upload the history
upload.summary: The analyst uploads a spreadsheet or CSV of the market's history — one row per period, one value per row.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: Market size requests arrive from different third-party sources every time and vary by request, so there is no single feed to connect. This was confirmed with the data science team; it is a deliberate choice, not a gap.

sections.heading: What it needs
items: Dates stamped at the end of each period — 31 January 2016, not 1 January 2016
A column of numbers. Text, footnote markers and blanks are handled

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: Nothing is calculated on upload. The work starts when the analyst presses Run analysis.

prepare.title: Check and choose
prepare.summary: The tool identifies the date and value columns, works out whether the data is weekly, monthly, quarterly or annual, and cleans it into one value per period with no gaps. The analyst then picks the models and how far ahead to project.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: Every model needs exactly one value per period with no holes. Two rows for March, or a missing April, breaks the arithmetic quietly rather than loudly.

sections.heading: What it does automatically
items: Reads real dates, bare years and quarter labels
Merges rows that share a period by adding them together
Fills the calendar so no period is missing
Reports how many rows it dropped and how many it merged

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: The cadence choice drives everything downstream — it sets the seasonal length the models look for.
If a file has one row per region per month, merging gives the national total. That may not be what was wanted.

macro.title: US macro drivers
macro.summary: 32 United States economic indicators are pulled from the Federal Reserve's public data service and tested to see which ones move ahead of this market.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: It is what lets one of the three models answer a what-if question rather than only extending a line.

sections.heading: What it covers
items: Employment, consumer spending, interest rates, confidence and related series
Only the indicators whose past movements actually help predict this market are kept

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: These are United States series. A UK or India market size has no appropriate driver here — the other two models still apply.
If the data service is unavailable, this model is skipped and the other two still run. The page says so.

modelA.title: With macro drivers (SARIMAX)
modelA.summary: Fits the market's history together with the economic indicators that were found to lead it.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: It is the only one of the three that can answer a scenario question, and the only one that gives a reason for the forecast rather than just a shape.

sections.heading: When to lean on it
items: When the market plausibly moves with employment, rates or consumer spending
When someone asks what happens if the economy softens

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: If it does not beat the history-only model, the economic drivers added nothing. That is a real finding.
The far end of its forecast is weaker than the near end, because the driver data runs out first.

modelB.title: History only (SARIMA)
modelB.summary: Fits the market using nothing but its own past. No outside data at all.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: It has no external dependency, so it cannot fail because someone else's service is down. It is also the fair baseline the macro model has to beat to justify its complexity.

sections.heading: When to lean on it
items: A stable, strongly seasonal market
Any non-US market size
When you need a number that will not change for infrastructure reasons

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: It cannot anticipate anything that has not already shown up in the history.

modelC.title: Trend shifts (Prophet)
modelC.summary: Splits the market into an underlying trend plus a repeating seasonal pattern, and reports the dates where the trend changed direction or pace.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: It catches trend breaks that the other two smooth over — the clearest example being 2020, which it is explicitly told about.

sections.heading: What it gives you
items: The dates the trend actually changed, which are directly quotable in a written market view
A forecast that does not assume the past rate of growth continues

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: Many trend changes on a short history usually means it is reading noise as signal.
It uses no economic data, so it cannot answer scenario questions.

answer.title: Score and compare
answer.summary: Every model is tested on recent periods it was never shown, then the three are put side by side and the spread between them is reported.

sections.heading: Why it is there
items: How well a model fits data it was trained on tells you almost nothing. Scoring on unseen periods is what makes the comparison meaningful, and the spread between three independent models is the closest thing here to an honest confidence statement.

sections.heading: How to read it
items: Models within 5% of each other — quote the midpoint as a working forecast
More than 5% apart — give a range and say the drivers need a look
Best means lowest error on history; it does not guarantee best in future

sections.heading: Watch out for
items: Always quote a band across the horizon, never a single number. The confidence interval is part of the answer.
Everything exports to one spreadsheet with lower and upper bounds per model.
